Which require NADPH?
I. HMG-CoA reductase
II. β-ketoacyl-ACP reductase
III. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
questions.why: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (III) uses biotin and ATP, not NADPH.

questions.stem:
Which favour fatty-acid oxidation over synthesis?
I. Glucagon
II. Insulin
III. Epinephrine
questions.why: Insulin (II) favours synthesis.

questions.stem:
Which are branch products of farnesyl pyrophosphate?
I. Ubiquinone
II. Dolichol
III. Haem a
questions.why: All three branch off before cholesterol.

questions.stem:
Which are true of acetyl-CoA carboxylase?
I. It is the rate-limiting enzyme
II. It requires biotin
III. It is inhibited by citrate
questions.why: Citrate (III) activates, not inhibits, the enzyme.

questions.stem:
Which describe β-oxidation?
I. It begins at the methyl end
II. It is mitochondrial
III. It uses FAD and NAD⁺
questions.why: β-oxidation begins at the carboxyl end (I is false).

questions.stem:
Which are basic amino acids?
I. Lysine
II. Arginine
III. Histidine
questions.why: All three are basic.

questions.stem:
Which are polar and uncharged?
I. Glutamate
II. Serine
III. Threonine
questions.why: Glutamate (I) is acidic and negatively charged.

questions.stem:
Which contain sulphur?
I. Cysteine
II. Methionine
III. Serine
questions.why: Serine (III) carries a hydroxyl, not sulphur.

questions.stem:
Which generally cannot be transaminated?
I. Lysine
II. Alanine
III. Threonine
questions.why: Alanine (II) is readily transaminated.

questions.stem:
Which are purely ketogenic amino acids?
I. Leucine
II. Valine
III. Isoleucine
questions.why: Valine is glucogenic and isoleucine is both; only leucine (I) is purely ketogenic.

questions.stem:
Which are products of amino-acid decarboxylation?
I. Histamine
II. Dopamine
III. Serotonin
questions.why: From histidine, DOPA and 5-hydroxytryptophan respectively.

questions.stem:
Which are acidic amino acids?
I. Asparagine
II. Aspartate
III. Glutamate
questions.why: Asparagine (I) is the uncharged amide of aspartate.

questions.stem:
Which absorb ultraviolet light at 280 nm?
I. Tryptophan
II. Tyrosine
III. Alanine
questions.why: Alanine (III) is not aromatic and does not absorb at 280 nm.

questions.stem:
Which are both glucogenic and ketogenic?
I. Isoleucine
II. Leucine
III. Phenylalanine
questions.why: Leucine (II) is purely ketogenic.

questions.stem:
Which are essential amino acids?
I. Valine
II. Alanine
III. Serine
questions.why: Alanine and serine are non-essential; only valine (I) is essential.

questions.stem:
Which are secreted as pancreatic zymogens?
I. Trypsinogen
II. Chymotrypsinogen
III. Pepsinogen
questions.why: Pepsinogen (III) is secreted by the stomach.

questions.stem:
Which are stabilised mainly by hydrogen bonds?
I. The primary sequence
II. The α-helix
III. The β-pleated sheet
questions.why: The primary sequence (I) is held by covalent peptide bonds.

questions.stem:
Which are eukaryotic cellular sources of reactive oxygen species?
I. Mitochondria
II. Peroxisomes
III. Endoplasmic reticulum
questions.why: All three generate ROS.

questions.stem:
Which are non-radical reactive species?
I. The hydroxyl radical
II. Hydrogen peroxide
III. Peroxynitrite
questions.why: The hydroxyl radical (I) is a true free radical.

questions.stem:
Which are reactive nitrogen species?
I. Nitric oxide
II. Peroxynitrite
III. The hydroxyl radical
questions.why: The hydroxyl radical (III) is a reactive oxygen species.

questions.stem:
Which are enzymatic antioxidants?
I. Superoxide dismutase
II. Vitamin E
III. Catalase
questions.why: Vitamin E (II) is a non-enzymatic antioxidant.

questions.stem:
Which are produced during the neutrophil respiratory burst?
I. Superoxide
II. Hydrogen peroxide
III. Hypochlorous acid
questions.why: Superoxide is made first, then H₂O₂, then hypochlorous acid.

questions.stem:
Which are biomarkers of lipid peroxidation?
I. Malondialdehyde
II. 8-hydroxydeoxyguanosine
III. Isoprostanes
questions.why: 8-hydroxydeoxyguanosine (II) is a marker of DNA oxidation.

questions.stem:
Which are dietary antioxidants?
I. Vitamin C
II. Vitamin E
III. Carotenoids
questions.why: All three are obtained from the diet.

questions.stem:
Which occur in the mitochondrial pathway of apoptosis?
I. Cytochrome c release
II. Caspase-9 activation
III. Synthesis of cytochrome c in the nucleus
questions.why: Cytochrome c is a mitochondrial protein, not made in the nucleus (III is false).

questions.stem:
Which are exogenous sources of free radicals?
I. Ultraviolet radiation
II. Mitochondrial respiration
III. Ionising radiation
questions.why: Mitochondrial respiration (II) is an endogenous source.

questions.stem:
Which take part in metal-catalysed radical generation?
I. Fe²⁺ in the Fenton reaction
II. Cu⁺ as a redox catalyst
III. Fe²⁺ acting as an antioxidant
questions.why: Iron is a pro-oxidant here, not an antioxidant (III is false).

questions.stem:
Which diseases are linked to oxidative stress?
I. Atherosclerosis
II. Parkinson’s disease
III. Diabetes mellitus
questions.why: All three are associated with reactive species.

questions.stem:
Which are true of superoxide dismutase?
I. It removes superoxide
II. It produces water
III. It produces hypochlorous acid
questions.why: SOD makes hydrogen peroxide, not water or hypochlorous acid; only I is true.

questions.why: Citrate activates fatty-acid synthesis; the others inhibit oxidation.

questions.stem: All of the following are made from cholesterol EXCEPT:
questions.why: Cholecystokinin is a gut peptide hormone, not a steroid.

questions.stem: All of the following are branched-chain amino acids EXCEPT:
questions.why: Methionine is a straight-chain, sulphur-containing amino acid.

questions.stem: All of the following are aromatic amino acids EXCEPT:
questions.why: Histidine is a basic amino acid.

questions.stem: All of the following are enzymatic antioxidants EXCEPT:
questions.why: α-Tocopherol (vitamin E) is a non-enzymatic antioxidant.

questions.stem: All of the following are essential amino acids EXCEPT:
questions.why: Alanine is non-essential.

questions.stem: All of the following are reactive oxygen species EXCEPT:
questions.why: Nitric oxide is a reactive nitrogen species.

questions.stem: All of the following are products of amino-acid decarboxylation EXCEPT:
questions.why: Urea is the product of the urea cycle, not decarboxylation.

questions.stem: All of the following are true of fatty-acid synthesis EXCEPT that it:
questions.why: Synthesis is cytosolic; the matrix is where oxidation occurs.

questions.stem: All of the following stabilise the tertiary structure of a protein EXCEPT:
questions.why: Peptide bonds link the backbone; they do not stabilise the fold itself.

questions.stem: All of the following are cellular sources of superoxide EXCEPT:
questions.why: Catalase removes hydrogen peroxide; it does not make superoxide.

questions.stem: Glucogenic amino acids may be catabolised to all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.why: Acetoacetyl-CoA is a ketogenic product.

questions.stem: All of the following are physiological functions of bile acids EXCEPT:
questions.why: Trypsinogen is activated by enteropeptidase, not by bile acids.

questions.stem: All of the following favour fatty-acid synthesis EXCEPT:
questions.why: Glucagon favours oxidation, not synthesis.

questions.stem: True or false: Fatty-acid synthesis uses NADPH as its reducing agent.
questions.why: It substitutes NADPH for the FADH₂ and NADH of oxidation.

questions.stem: True or false: Palmitate is the only fatty acid made by the fatty acid synthase complex.
questions.why: Longer fatty acids come from the elongation system.

questions.stem: True or false: All reactive oxygen species are free radicals.
questions.why: Hydrogen peroxide is a ROS with no unpaired electron.

questions.stem: True or false: Glycine is optically active.
questions.why: Its side chain is a hydrogen, so it has no chiral centre.

questions.stem: True or false: Essential amino acids can be synthesised by the human body.
questions.why: By definition they cannot be made and must be eaten.

questions.stem: True or false: Glutamate dehydrogenase is inhibited by GTP and ATP.
questions.why: GDP and ADP are its activators.

questions.stem: True or false: The hydroxyl radical can be generated by the Fenton reaction.
questions.why: Ferrous iron reacts with hydrogen peroxide.

questions.stem: True or false: Lysine and threonine readily undergo transamination.
questions.why: They are the two amino acids generally not transaminated.

questions.stem: Which enzyme catalyses the first step of the hepatic urea cycle?
questions.why: CPS1 forms carbamoyl phosphate within mitochondria (S23).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: Carbamoyl phosphate condenses with ornithine to form which intermediate?
questions.why: Ornithine transcarbamoylase catalyses citrulline synthesis (S24).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: In the third urea-cycle reaction, citrulline combines with aspartate to form:
questions.why: Argininosuccinate synthetase forms argininosuccinate in cytosol (S25).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: The products of argininosuccinate lyase are:
questions.why: Argininosuccinate lyase releases fumarate and arginine (S25).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: Arginase catalyses the production of:
questions.why: Hydrolysis of arginine completes the urea cycle (S25).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: Which compound is the direct allosteric activator of CPS1?
questions.why: N-acetylglutamate activates CPS1 (S23, S29).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: The enzyme synthesising N-acetylglutamate is stimulated by:
questions.why: Arginine enhances NAGS activity (S23, S29).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: Which blood test pairing matches the lecture?
questions.why: BUN reflects renal function; blood ammonia reflects liver function (S22).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: The most prominent carrier of ammonia from tissues to the kidney is:
questions.why: Glutamine is the major NH₃ carrier in blood to the kidneys (S10).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: Renal glutaminase initially converts glutamine into:
questions.why: Glutaminase releases one NH₃ and generates glutamate (S10).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: Which metabolite becomes depleted when excess ammonia drives the glutamate dehydrogenase reaction in reverse?
questions.why: Ammonia S14: reversal consumes α-ketoglutarate, lowering ATP synthesis.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: In skeletal muscle, ammonia is carried to the liver mainly as:
questions.why: Alanine transports nitrogen during the glucose–alanine cycle (S13).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: Which enzyme can release a second mole of ammonia from glutamate in the kidney?
questions.why: GDH converts glutamate to α-ketoglutarate (S10).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: Which process becomes impaired when high ammonia levels deplete ATP?
questions.why: Lower ATP depresses active transport and neuronal electrochemical gradients (S14).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: Which of the following is a symptom of urea-cycle-defect hyperammonaemia?
questions.why: The lecture lists lethargy, stupor, convulsions and CNS impairment (S28).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem:
Assertion: Astrocytic glutamine synthetase helps protect neurons from excitotoxicity.
Reason: It converts excess ammonia and neurotoxic glutamate into glutamine.
questions.why: This astrocyte reaction is directly protective (S7).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem:
Assertion: BUN is used to assess kidney function.
Reason: Glucose–alanine cycling carries muscle nitrogen to the liver.
questions.why: Both are true, but the cycle is not the reason for the BUN test (S13, S22).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem:
Assertion: Ornithine transcarbamoylase functions within mitochondria.
Reason: Citrulline is transported from cytosol into mitochondria.
questions.why: OTC is mitochondrial, but citrulline actually moves out into the cytosol (S22–S24).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem:
Which urea-cycle statements are correct?
I. CPS1 operates in mitochondria.
II. Argininosuccinate lyase releases fumarate.
III. Arginase forms urea.
questions.why: All three match the five-step sequence (S23–S25).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem:
Which nitrogen-excretion classifications are correct?
I. Birds are ureotelic.
II. Bony fishes are ammonotelic.
III. Reptiles are uricotelic.
questions.why: Bony fishes excrete ammonia; reptiles and birds excrete uric acid (S19).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: All of the following are urea-cycle intermediates EXCEPT:
questions.why: Homogentisate belongs to tyrosine catabolism, not the urea cycle (S21; carbon catabolism S33).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: True or false: During urea synthesis, citrulline moves from cytosol into mitochondria.
questions.why: Citrulline instead moves from mitochondria into cytosol (S22, S24).
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: The lecture estimates that how much BCAA transamination occurs in skeletal muscle?
questions.why: The skeletal-muscle share is approximately 65% (S6).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem: The second shared step of leucine, isoleucine and valine catabolism is catalysed by:
questions.why: The BCKD complex oxidatively decarboxylates the three α-keto acids (S7–S8).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem: The common branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase complex is inactivated by:
questions.why: BCKD becomes inactive when phosphorylated (S10).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem: The odour of urine and sweat characteristic of maple syrup urine disease is:
questions.why: The urine and sweat have a maple-syrup odour (S13).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem: Some cases of maple syrup urine disease respond to high doses of:
questions.why: Thiamine responsiveness is noted for some MSUD cases (S13).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem: A less severe BCKD deficiency with symptoms appearing intermittently is called:
questions.why: This MSUD variant shows a less severe deficiency and later episodic symptoms (S15).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem: Isovaleric acidaemia involves deficiency of which enzyme?
questions.why: Isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase is required for leucine catabolism (S16).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem: An infant develops a cheesy breath odour, vomiting and acidosis after protein feeds. The lecture associates this with:
questions.why: Protein-triggered vomiting/acidosis and cheesy odour are described (S16).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem: Phenylalanine hydroxylase requires which cofactor?
questions.why: Phenylalanine hydroxylation uses tetrahydrobiopterin (S19).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem: The phenylalanine hydroxylase gene involved in PKU lies on:
questions.why: The lecture identifies chromosome 12 (S18).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem: Type I tyrosinaemia is caused by deficiency of:
questions.why: Fumarylacetoacetase is the deficient enzyme (S28).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem: Type II tyrosinaemia involves a defect in:
questions.why: This deficiency causes the ocular and cutaneous syndrome (S30–S31).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem: Type III tyrosinaemia involves deficiency of:
questions.why: Type III involves 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (S32).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem: The urinary compound oxidising to a dark pigment in alkaptonuria is:
questions.why: Homogentisate oxidises into dark alkapton pigment (S33, S43).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem: Histidinaemia is associated with deficiency of:
questions.why: Histidine ammonia lyase deficiency is named in the lecture (S42).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem:
Assertion: Type II tyrosinaemia can cause painful skin lesions on palms and soles.
Reason: It involves deficiency of tyrosine aminotransferase.
questions.why: The type II enzyme defect underlies the ocular and skin syndrome (S30–S31).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem:
Assertion: Some MSUD patients improve after high-dose thiamine.
Reason: Histidinaemia may produce elevated blood histidine.
questions.why: Both facts are true, but the histidine change does not explain thiamine response (S13, S42).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem:
Assertion: Type I tyrosinaemia is due to defective histidine ammonia lyase.
Reason: Type I tyrosinaemia may cause liver disease in infants.
questions.why: Type I reflects fumarylacetoacetase deficiency; liver disease is a manifestation (S28–S29).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem:
Which disease–defect pairings are correct?
I. MSUD — branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase.
II. Isovaleric acidaemia — tyrosine aminotransferase.
III. Type III tyrosinaemia — 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase.
questions.why: I and III match the lecture; isovaleric acidaemia affects isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase (S10, S16, S32).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem:
Which clinical features of type III tyrosinaemia are taught?
I. Seizures.
II. Intermittent ataxia.
III. Cheesy odour of breath.
questions.why: Seizures and ataxia are described for type III; cheesy breath is linked to isovaleric acidaemia (S16, S32).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem: All of these belong to the management of PKU in the lecture EXCEPT:
questions.why: PKU management requires controlled phenylalanine, not unrestricted protein (S20–S21).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem: True or false: Type II tyrosinaemia is referred to as Richner–Hanhart syndrome.
questions.why: The lecture uses Richner–Hanhart for type II (S31).
questions.subtopic: Amino acid catabolism and inborn errors

questions.stem: Methionine provides the principal methyl donor for biosynthesis in the form of:
questions.why: S-adenosylmethionine is the principal methyl donor (S4).

questions.stem: The PLP-dependent enzyme that converts homocysteine to cystathionine is:
questions.why: CBS catalyses the irreversible transsulfuration step (S5).

questions.stem: The action of cystathionine γ-lyase produces cysteine and:
questions.why: Cystathionine produces cysteine and α-ketobutyrate (S5).

questions.stem: In the lecture, α-ketobutyric acid is further oxidatively decarboxylated to:
questions.why: α-Ketobutyrate forms propionyl-CoA (S8).

questions.stem: The primary deficient enzyme described in homocystinuria is:
questions.why: CBS deficiency increases blood homocysteine and methionine (S9).

questions.stem: In homocystinuria, homocysteine disrupts which structural process?
questions.why: Homocysteine interferes with collagen cross-linking (S10).

questions.stem: In the methionine lecture, atheroma formation is linked to homocysteine-thiolactone-driven:
questions.why: Homocysteine thiolactone modifies LDL and favours its aggregation (S10).

questions.stem: A recognised ophthalmological presentation of homocystinuria is:
questions.why: Bilateral lens dislocation is listed (S11).

questions.stem: Which diet change is recommended in homocystinuria?
questions.why: Methionine restriction plus extra cysteine is recommended (S12).

questions.stem: Cystathionuria is associated with deficiency of:
questions.why: γ-Lyase deficiency or insufficient PLP can cause cystathionuria (S13).

questions.stem: According to the lecture, the major cysteine catabolic pathway leads to formation of:
questions.why: The major three-step cysteine degradation pathway yields pyruvate (S15).

questions.stem: Taurine conjugation with bile acids assists hepatic clearance of:
questions.why: Taurine conjugation enhances cholesterol clearance (S17).

questions.stem: The mitochondrial enzyme converting sulfite into sulfate is:
questions.why: Sulfite oxidase catalyses this conversion (S18).

questions.stem: PAPS acts as a donor of which group in biological systems?
questions.why: PAPS supplies sulfate groups for biosynthetic reactions (S18–S19).

questions.stem: Biotin can be sequestered by avidin present in:
questions.why: The lecture identifies avidin in uncooked egg white (S24).

questions.stem:
Assertion: Homocystinuria may cause connective-tissue abnormalities.
Reason: Homocysteine accumulation interferes with collagen cross-linking.
questions.why: This is the lecture's mechanism of connective-tissue injury (S10).

questions.stem:
Assertion: Biotin participates in carboxylation reactions.
Reason: Avidin from uncooked egg white can sequester biotin.
questions.why: Both facts are true, but avidin binding does not explain biotin carboxylation (S24).

questions.stem:
Assertion: Tetrahydrofolate transports only carbon dioxide.
Reason: S-adenosylmethionine is the main donor of sulfate groups.
questions.why: Both claims are false: THF carries various one-carbon units and SAM donates methyl groups (S4, S22–S23).

questions.stem:
Which molecules are one-carbon transfer cofactors in the lecture?
I. Biotin.
II. Tetrahydrofolate.
III. S-adenosylmethionine.
questions.why: All three are explicitly listed (S22).

questions.stem:
Which features are described in homocystinuria?
I. Spinal deformation.
II. Maple-syrup urine odour.
III. Cheesy-smelling urine.
questions.why: Only spinal deformation is listed for homocystinuria; the odours distinguish MSUD and isovaleric acidaemia (S10; carbon catabolism S13, S16).

questions.stem: All of these are products or intermediates of cysteine metabolism EXCEPT:
questions.why: Cysteine can yield sulfinate, hypotaurine, pyruvate and thiosulfate; argininosuccinate is in the urea cycle (S15–S21; ammonia S25).

questions.stem: True or false: Cystathionuria causes a loss of cystathionine from both blood and urine.
questions.why: Cystathionine instead accumulates in blood and is excreted in urine (S13).

questions.stem: The liver's ability to scavenge ammonia not incorporated into urea depends on:

options.label: A
options.text: a uniform distribution of all enzymes in the liver

options.label: B
options.text: absence of the enzyme glutamine synthetase

options.label: C
options.text: different cellular sites for glutaminase and synthetase

options.label: D
options.text: exclusive mitochondrial location of all urea enzymes

options.label: E
options.text: cessation of glutamine formation during protein feeding

options.label: A
options.text: raise hepatic urea formation while conserving bicarbonate

options.text: conserve bicarbonate otherwise required in urea synthesis

options.label: C
options.text: reduce urinary ammonium excretion while saving bicarbonate

options.label: D
options.text: promote liver glutaminase without increasing bicarbonate use

options.label: E
options.text: increase liver ureogenesis while reducing renal ammonia

questions.why: Ammonia S10: ammonia ionises to NH₄⁺ before excretion.

questions.why: Ammonia S12: liver mitochondrial glutaminase converts glutamine to glutamate.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: The inhibitory effect of excess ammonia on neurotransmitter synthesis involves:
questions.why: Ammonia S14: GABA synthesis may be impeded.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: The abnormal production of which compound is implicated in ammonia-associated encephalopathy?
questions.why: Ammonia S15: increased glutamine formation may lead to encephalopathy.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.why: Ammonia S15: Na⁺–K⁺ ATPase inhibition is specified.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: One source of alanine released from skeletal muscle, besides pyruvate transamination, is:
questions.why: Ammonia S17: alanine arises from protein degradation or pyruvate transamination.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.why: Ammonia S17: ALT is also called SGPT.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: In the glucose–alanine cycle, hepatic pyruvate supplies:
questions.why: Ammonia S13 and S16: the liver converts pyruvate to glucose for muscle.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: Alanine ranks second in circulating prominence to which amino acid?
questions.why: Ammonia S17: alanine is second only to glutamine.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: The urea-cycle intermediate released in the argininosuccinate-lyase reaction that enters mitochondria is:
questions.why: Ammonia S26: fumarate is transported into mitochondria.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: Fumarate is converted ultimately into oxaloacetate through the actions of:
questions.why: Ammonia S26: fumarase and malate dehydrogenase are involved.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.why: Ammonia S26: oxaloacetate is converted to the nitrogen donor aspartate.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I utilises which energy substrate combination?
questions.why: Ammonia S27: NH₄⁺ + HCO₃⁻ + 2ATP are the reactants.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: The ATP-derived products of argininosuccinate synthesis are:
questions.why: Ammonia S27: ASS yields AMP and PPᵢ.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: With complete absence of a urea-synthesising enzyme, an infant may die:

options.label: C
options.text: soon after the first protein meal

options.label: D
options.text: only with severe vitamin C depletion

questions.why: Ammonia S28: the first protein meal can precipitate fatal hyperammonaemia.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: The lecture describes which dietary substitution in inherited urea-cycle defects?

options.label: B
options.text: α-keto analogues of essential amino acids

questions.why: Ammonia S28: α-keto analogues of essential amino acids are given.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: N-acetylglutamate synthase is stimulated or supplied by which substrate besides arginine?
questions.why: Ammonia S29: glutamate is a NAGS substrate and activator.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: Which hormones are named as regulators of hepatic urea-cycle enzyme expression?
questions.why: Ammonia S30: glucagon, insulin and glucocorticoids regulate expression.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: Citrullinaemia reflects deficiency of which enzyme?
questions.why: Ammonia S31: ASS defect is citrullinaemia.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle

questions.stem: Argininosuccinic acidemia reflects deficiency of which enzyme?
questions.why: Ammonia S31: ASL deficiency gives argininosuccinic acidemia.
questions.subtopic: Ammonia transport and the urea cycle
